snippet.title: Up when your eyes open
snippet.description:
Any morning: when your eyes open, feet on the floor. Sitting counts. Before the phone, before the list. Closer to your body.

A story built on a real morning: he sits up before he thinks. His mind gets a vote later. Some mornings he lies there one more breath.

That foggy first stretch after waking has a name, sleep inertia, and a 2019 review found it is strongest in the first 30 minutes (Hilditch and McHill, Nature and Science of Sleep, https://doi.org/10.2147/NSS.S188911). We know of no study on sitting up first. One first minute, nothing more.

If standing up makes you dizzy, go slowly: lying, then sitting, then standing. If it keeps happening, tell your doctor. (NHS, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-pressure-hypotension/)

From the Sleep door. New ones come out on set days; this one works any morning.

Best with headphones.

3D audio (HRTF: MIT KEMAR, Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994)

snippet.title: Call, don't type
snippet.description:
When you start to type, press call. Ten seconds counts. If no one picks up, that counts too.

Closer to yourself. Closer to your people.

Two researchers asked people to reconnect with an old friend, some by phone and some by email. Most guessed the call would be more awkward. It was no more awkward than the email, and the people who called felt a stronger bond (Kumar and Epley, 2021, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General). We read the abstract and two summaries, not the full paper.

Driving? Call when you've parked.

Best with headphones.

snippet.title: How to use NAOS. Any door, any day.
snippet.description:
NAOS is a toolbox of small behaviors, each with the moment to use it. The videos show them. The page keeps them, open any day.

The doors, with one example each:
Move: when the coffee drips, move for two minutes, at your pace.
Breathe: when a message tightens your jaw, two in through the nose, one long out.
Eat: when the plate lands, one breath before the first bite.
Sleep: when your eyes open, feet on the floor.
Community: about to type to someone? Press call.
The Divine: after dark, look up once.
The week: one card that holds the whole week.

Behind each door: the behavior, its moment, a question, a short scene and a tool to take with you. Any door fits any moment, and what you need will change.

The day of the week only tells you when each door gets something new:
Mon Move · Tue Breathe · Wed Eat · Thu Sleep · Fri Community · Sat The week · Sun The Divine

How to use NAOS: watch a Short, open the page, pick the door you need right now, take the tool.

Why each behavior comes with its moment: across 94 tests, plans that say when and where you'll act helped people reach their goals (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006).
The Breathe example is called cyclic sighing, one of three practices in a month-long study that measured mood and breathing rate (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895
The study practiced five minutes a day; once is the short version.
The moon on The Divine door is the real one for 24 October: full on 26 October, 04:12 UTC (U.S. Naval Observatory).

Breathe normally if you feel light-headed. If moving hurts, stop.

The tools: https://hardlypythonnmr.github.io/naos/

Best with headphones. HRTF: MIT KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994).

snippet.title: Hold the first bite
snippet.description:
About to eat? A tool for the first bite: a breath, and someone in mind.

When the plate lands, hold the first bite. One breath, one name. Who comes to mind? Say it, or just think it. Then go ahead.

Eating with someone? They can hold it too.

Why a when: a review of 94 tests found that plans shaped "when this happens, I'll do that" helped people follow through on what they meant to do (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006). No study we know of has tested this one at a table. It's a bet.

Next on this table: Who taught you to give thanks?

Best with headphones.

Sources:
Gollwitzer PM and Sheeran P (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38, 69-119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1

More on this table: https://hardlypythonnmr.github.io/naos/temas/the-full-moon-table/

HRTF: MIT KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994)

snippet.title: Full tomorrow: look up once
snippet.description:
Stepping out tonight? Look up once. When you step outside after dark: one breath, eyes up. Clouds count too.

What did you notice first?

Closer to yourself. Closer to the divine.

The moon is full on Sunday night, Oct 25 (00:12 ET Monday; 23:12 in Medellín), per the U.S. Naval Observatory. On Saturday, Oct 24, it's about 97% lit and already up when it gets dark.

Sixty older adults were asked to take a 15-minute walk each week for eight weeks. One group was also asked to look for something vast and new, if possible. In the 52 whose photos were analyzed, that group filled less of their own photos with themselves and more with what was around them over the weeks, compared with the other walkers (Sturm and colleagues, 2022, Emotion). We read the full paper.

Not while driving or crossing a street. Look up where you can stand still.

Best with headphones.

Sources:
Moon phase and rise times: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/MoonPhases
Sturm VE and colleagues (2022). Big smile, small self: Awe walks promote prosocial positive emotions in older adults. Emotion 22(5), 1044-1058. https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000876

snippet.title: One breath before the first bite
snippet.description:
Dinner on the table? A tool for the first bite: one breath, one name. When the plate lands, hold the first bite. Who comes to mind? Then eat.

The tale: on Sharad Purnima, the full moon of Ashvin at the end of the monsoon, many Hindu homes and temples set kheer (rice, milk and sugar) out in the moonlight for the whole night. In the morning it is eaten and shared as prasad: offered first, then shared (Drik Panchang; eSamskriti, from Bhavan's Journal; BAPS Swaminarayan). Not every family sets out the same thing, and the date depends on where you are and which rule your family keeps: Drik Panchang puts it on Sunday 25 October in New York, Medellín and Delhi. Corrections welcome.

We don't ask anyone to leave food out overnight, or to fast. Your plate is for tonight's dinner.

Best with headphones.

Sources:
Drik Panchang, Sharad Purnima 2026: https://www.drikpanchang.com/purnima/sharad/sharad-purnima-date-time.html?year=2026&geoname-id=1261481
eSamskriti, About Sharad Purnima: https://www.esamskriti.com/e/Culture/Festivals/About-Sharad-Purnima-1.aspx

snippet.title: Primero, comer con alguien
snippet.description:
¿Vas a comer? La idea: la próxima comida, con alguien. Piensa en alguien, cerca o a una llamada, y escríbele: ¿comemos juntos? O mándale este video. ¿Te dijo que no? Todo bien: pregúntale a otra persona. Cuando llega el plato, el celular boca abajo y una respiración.

Más cerca de ti. Más cerca de los tuyos.

Latinoamérica y el Caribe son la región del mundo donde más se comparte la mesa: unos 9 de los 14 almuerzos y cenas de la semana, con familia, amigos o alguien conocido, según la Encuesta Mundial de Gallup de 2022 y 2023 (World Happiness Report 2025, capítulo 3: De Neve, Dugan, Kaats y Prati). Los autores dicen que no pueden afirmar qué causa qué. El módulo de la encuesta lo financió el grupo Ajinomoto.
Fuente: https://worldhappiness.report/ed/2025/sharing-meals-with-others-how-sharing-meals-supports-happiness-and-social-connections/ (doi:10.18724/whr-g119-bv60)

¿Comes sin compañía? Una llamada mientras comes también cuenta.

Si esto te está pesando, no lo cargues a solas: háblalo con alguien de confianza o con un profesional de salud mental. Si estás pensando en hacerte daño, llama ya a una línea de ayuda: Colombia 106 (Minsalud, 24 h) o 123 si hay peligro inmediato · México 800 911 2000 (Línea de la Vida) · España 024 · EE. UU. 988 y marca 2 · Argentina 135 o (011) 5275-1135 · otros países: findahelpline.com

Mejor con audífonos.

snippet.title: Lower your phone. Look up once.
snippet.description:
Dark out yet? A tool for after dark: one breath, and the sky. Lower your phone. Step outside, or find a window. If it's cloudy, look up anyway.

When you step outside after dark, look up once. Then ask one person: did you see it?

Closer to yourself. Closer to the divine.

Full on Sunday night, October 25: 23:12 in Colombia, just after midnight in New York (04:12 UTC, October 26, US Naval Observatory). A full moon rises around sunset, opposite the sun. The same side of the moon faces Earth all the time (NASA), and likely has for billions of years (Alan Boss in Scientific American).

Not while driving or crossing a street. Look up where you can see your footing.

Best with headphones.

Sources:
Full moon time: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/MoonPhases
Same face, full moon at sunset: NASA Science, Moon Facts, https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/ and Moon Phases, https://science.nasa.gov/moon/moon-phases/
Billions of years: Alan P. Boss, Scientific American, https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/is-it-just-a-coincidence/

https://hardlypythonnmr.github.io/naos

HRTF: MIT KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994)

snippet.title: Physiological sigh before you open the door
snippet.description:
A physiological sigh before you open the door: two breaths in through your nose, one long breath out. One round, quicker than finding your keys.
The pattern is also called cyclic sighing. In a month-long study, people did it five minutes a day, and the researchers measured mood and breathing rate (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895

First a slow breath in. A second one fills the rest. Then out, slow, all the way down. The second breath in can be briefer than the first. This video does one round.

If you feel light-headed, breathe normally. Never force the second breath, and don't hold it.
The study excluded people with heart disease, pregnancy, a history of seizures and some psychiatric conditions. If one applies to you, ask your doctor first.

Best with headphones.

HRTF: MIT KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994)

snippet.title: Movement snacks: find the moment
snippet.description:
Movement snacks, also called exercise snacks: two minutes of moving inside a moment you already have, like the coffee dripping.
Roll your shoulders, reach up, walk to the window and back. Your pace. A chair is fine. Closer to your body.

Been still too long? A two minute movement break can hang on something that already happens in your day. When the coffee drips: move for two minutes. Or when a call ends. Any moment that's yours.

The WHO says all physical activity counts, and any amount is better than none. Its 2020 guidelines recommend at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity a week for adults. (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity · https://www.who.int/news/item/25-11-2020-every-move-counts-towards-better-health-says-who)

For us, two minutes is a first step toward that.

Habit research suggests picking a cue inside a routine you already have, like the coffee dripping, and repeating the action in that same context (Gardner, Lally and Wardle, British Journal of General Practice, 2012, https://doi.org/10.3399/bjgp12X659466).

If it hurts, stop. If you have a health condition, check with your doctor about what's right for you.

From the Move door. New tools come out on set days; this one works any day.

Best with headphones.

The second breath in can be shorter than the first, and you exhale longer than you inhale. One sigh is the short version.

snippet.title: Movement snacks: I don't wait for the gym
snippet.description:
Movement snacks, also called exercise snacks, are short stretches of moving, two minutes at a time. This one starts when the coffee drips.
Waiting for a free hour to move? You already have two minutes. Think of it as a 2 minute movement break, any time something makes you wait.

When the coffee drips, move for two minutes. Or the kettle. Or the elevator. Any wait works. At your pace.

Closer to your body. Closer to yourself.

We made up this story. The rule in it is real: until 2020, the WHO guidelines asked adults to count aerobic activity in stretches of at least 10 minutes. The 2020 guidelines dropped that rule: moderate to vigorous movement of any length now counts toward the weekly target (150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity, or 75 to 150 of vigorous, or a mix; Bull et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955). The WHO puts it plainly: all physical activity counts (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity).

If it hurts, stop. If you have a health condition, check with your doctor first.

Best with headphones.

snippet.description:
About to eat? In about six minutes: the whole tool (when the plate lands, hold the first bite, one breath, one name, then eat), your own if-then plan said out loud, how it works alone, with others and under tonight's full moon, and one round together, today.

When the plate lands: one breath, one name.
Tonight: set one more plate. Look up first.

Chapters
0:00 The whole tool in ten seconds
0:36 The shape: hold, one breath, one name
1:10 When to use it: the second the plate lands
1:40 Why a when works, and how much
2:45 Make your own plan, out loud
3:12 Alone or with others
3:50 Tonight: the full-moon table
4:40 What to notice, and the five-second version
5:12 One round together, in real time
6:05 Your card, and one question

A behavior to try, with no promise about digestion, weight or calm. No fasting and no food left out overnight: your plate is for dinner.

Sources, in the order they appear
Why a when (if-then plans, 94 tests, d = 0.65): Gollwitzer PM, Sheeran P. Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
The honest part (a close cousin, mental contrasting with implementation intentions: 21 papers, 24 comparisons, 15,907 people, g = 0.34, about 0.24 after correcting for publication bias; face-to-face plans did better than plans made from a page): Wang G, Wang Y, Gai X. snippet.title: Physiological sigh: two in, one out, before you answer
snippet.description:
Physiological sigh (cyclic sighing): two in through the nose, one long out. The shape, the moment to use it, and five rounds together.
Did the last message you read tighten your jaw? Here is one small thing to try before you answer, in under six minutes.

When a message tightens your jaw: two in, one out.

Chapters
0:00 The whole tool in ten seconds
0:28 The shape: slow, deeper, long
1:10 When to use it: before you answer
1:41 Why your body already knows it
2:42 What to notice, and the one-round version
3:13 Five rounds together, in real time
4:40 What the 2023 study measured
5:19 Your card, and one question

If you feel light-headed, stop and breathe normally. Never force the second breath, and never hold it. Never while driving. A practice, not therapy.
The study excluded people with heart disease, pregnancy, a history of seizures and some psychiatric conditions. If one applies to you, ask your doctor first.

Sources, in the order they appear
The shape (cyclic sighing) and what was measured: Balban MY et al. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Reports Medicine, 2023. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895
A month, 108 people in four practices, five minutes a day; mood before and after, and breathing rate. The study was exploratory and not pre-registered as a clinical trial. Five rounds is the short version.

snippet.title: How to use NAOS: cyclic sighing in 10 seconds, then every door
snippet.description:
How to use NAOS: cyclic sighing (two in, one out) in 10 seconds, then the seven doors where every small tool lives.
A guided cyclic sighing round, why each small behavior comes with its moment (if-then plans), how long habits take, and the page that keeps every tool open, any day.

Sources (the citations on screen)
1. Cyclic sighing, the two-in-one-out breath: one of three breathing practices in a month-long study that measured mood and breathing rate. Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895 The study practiced five minutes a day; one round is the short version.
2. Why each behavior comes with its moment: across 94 tests, plans that say when and where you'll act (implementation intentions) helped people reach their goals. Gollwitzer and Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
3. How long a habit takes: 96 volunteers each chose one eating, drinking or activity behavior to do daily in the same context for 12 weeks. The time to reach 95% of their own limit of automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days, and missing one opportunity did not materially affect the process. Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674

Chapters
0:00 What you'll get, and what NAOS is
0:38 Your first tool: two in, one out
1:45 Why every tool comes with a moment
2:48 Six more doors, each one working
4:01 Any door, any day
4:29 Where the tools live
4:59 Your first door, today

NAOS is a toolbox of small behaviors for the basics of being human: eating, sleeping, moving, your people, the divine, and under all of them, your breath. Each tool is one small behavior with the moment to use it.

Pick a door. Take one behavior and its moment. Repeat it.

The doors, with the tool in this video:
Breathe: when a message tightens your jaw, two in through the nose, one long out (cyclic sighing).
Eat: when the plate lands, one breath, one name.
Sleep: when your eyes open, feet on the floor. Sitting counts.
Move: when the coffee drips, a two-minute movement snack. Walk, stretch, your pace.
Community: when you start to type to someone, press call. Ten seconds counts.
The Divine: when you step outside after dark, look up once.
The week: when the week ends, which one stayed?

Any door fits any day. The days only tell you when something new arrives:
Mon Move · Tue Breathe · Wed Eat · Thu Sleep · Fri Community · Sat The week · Sun The Divine

The tools: https://hardlypythonnmr.github.io/naos/

Which door will you start with: the one you need most, or the one that's easiest?

If you feel light-headed, stop and breathe normally. Never force the second breath, and never hold it. If moving hurts, stop. Looking up: look where you can see your footing. Driving? Look when you've parked. A practice. For health questions, talk to a professional.

The moon on The Divine door is the real one for the night of 24 October: full on 26 October, 04:12 UTC (U.S. Naval Observatory).

Best with headphones.

HRTF: MIT KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, MIT Media Lab, 1994)
